operations.evidence: Charge or summons outcomes for non-victim-based offences took a median of 40 days.
Processing time does not represent parcel-level public-safety conditions.
Drug offence charge or summons outcomes took 53 days, down from 62 days.
Drug offence volumes and outcomes are highly influenced by enforcement activity.
Possession of weapons charge or summons outcomes took 18 days, down from 22 days.
This outcome timing does not locate offences or quantify local exposure.
Public order charge or summons outcomes took 28 days, down from 36 days.
Changes can reflect operational and case-mix effects.
Around 12.9% of offences involving a firearm resulted in a charge or summons, up from 12.0%.
Firearm involvement is a cross-cutting subset and the rate is not a local risk score.
Around 13.0% of knife-enabled offences resulted in a charge or summons, up from 11.5%.
Knife-enabled outcomes must not be interpreted as exact-location evidence.
The knife-enabled charge or summons rate of 13.0% was higher than the 7.5% rate for equivalent offences not involving a knife.
Differences may reflect offence seriousness, evidence, and investigation selection.
The bulletin covers all territorial police forces in England and Wales and British Transport Police.
National coverage does not guarantee uniform recording quality across forces.
The current crime outcomes framework was introduced in April 2013, replacing the narrower detections framework.
Long-term comparisons across framework changes require caution.
The main outcomes data are a snapshot of the case status of offences recorded during the year ending March 2026.
Cases still open at the snapshot date can change outcome later.
Police forces submit revised data as investigations are completed, so previously published outcomes can be revised.
First-release figures are not final for complex offences.
For statistical purposes, every recorded crime is assigned one outcome type.
One outcome category does not capture every investigative action or later justice result.
Open data tables publish the full range of police outcome types beyond grouped bulletin categories.
Open data availability does not remove disclosure, quality, or comparability limitations.
Approximately 12.6% of victim-based charge outcomes related to an alternative offence to the one originally recorded.
The centrally held data cannot identify the specific alternative offence charged.
Approximately 4.8% of non-victim-based charge outcomes related to an alternative offence.
Alternative-offence rates should not be used to infer local offending patterns.
Around 4.4 million victim-based offences were recorded in the 12 months to March 2026, 2% fewer than the previous year.
Recorded volume is affected by reporting and recording practices.
At year-end, 6.9% of victim-based offences remained under investigation, down from 7.9%.
Open-case shares depend on offence complexity and recording date.
The volume of charge or summons outcomes for victim-based offences rose 12.8%, from 345,521 to 389,728.
Outcome volume is not directly comparable with crime prevalence.
The victim-based charge or summons proportion increased from 6.3% to 7.3%.
Year-end proportions are incomplete where many investigations remain open.
The victim-based charge or summons proportion fell from 11.1% in the year ending March 2016 to 4.6% in the year ending March 2022 before the recent rise.
Framework, recording, case-mix, and investigation changes limit causal interpretation.
